subject: Medicine
summary: Giardiasis is a water‑borne protozoal infection causing acute or chronic watery diarrhoea, malabsorption and weight loss. Diagnosis relies on stool microscopy or antigen testing, and treatment is with nitroimidazoles.

sections.p: Giardiasis is infection of the upper small intestine by the flagellated protozoan Giardia. Diagnosis requires detection of the organism or its antigens in stool, or duodenal aspirate when stool is negative.
b: Microscopic identification of cysts or trophozoites in ≥3 stool samples
Enzyme immunoassay (EIA) or rapid antigen test on stool
String test (Enterotest) or duodenal biopsy if stool studies are inconclusive

sections.p: Severity is graded by symptom burden and impact on nutrition rather than a formal stage system. Mild disease: intermittent diarrhoea, no weight loss. Moderate: daily diarrhoea, abdominal cramping, weight loss <5 %. Severe: persistent watery diarrhoea >2 weeks, dehydration, >5 % weight loss, or malabsorption requiring parenteral nutrition.
b: Assess dehydration, weight loss, and duration of symptoms
Consider immune status (HIV, malnutrition) for severity

sections.p: Giardia is acquired by ingesting cysts from contaminated water, food, or person‑to‑person spread. In low‑resource settings, outbreaks follow unsafe water supplies; in travelers, untreated mountain streams are common sources.
b: Contaminated drinking water (most common)
Fruits/vegetables washed with unsafe water
Person‑to‑person transmission in childcare settings
Travel to endemic regions

sections.p: Patients develop watery, foul‑smelling diarrhoea, often with greasy stools, abdominal bloating, flatulence, and crampy pain. Chronic infection may cause weight loss, fatigue, and nutrient deficiencies (especially fat‑soluble vitamins).
b: Diarrhoea 1–2 weeks after exposure
Steatorrhea and malabsorption
Possible low‑grade fever, nausea

sections.p: Targeted tests confirm the parasite and assess complications such as dehydration or malabsorption.

t.b: Does the stool contain Giardia? Positive confirms infection.
Is Giardia antigen present? Higher sensitivity; a positive result confirms infection.
Can intermittent shedding be caught? Multiple samples increase detection.
Is the patient dehydrated? Abnormal values guide rehydration.
Is malabsorption significant? Elevated fat indicates need for nutritional support.

sections.p: Complications are uncommon but can be life‑threatening in vulnerable patients.
b: Severe dehydration or electrolyte imbalance
Persistent weight loss >10 % in children
Acute renal failure from volume loss
Secondary bacterial infection

sections.p: Treat the parasite, replace fluids, and correct malabsorption. First‑line therapy is a nitroimidazole; alternatives are used when resistance or intolerance is suspected.
b: Nitroimidazole (e.g., metronidazole) – kills trophozoites and cysts; chosen for proven efficacy
Tinidazole – similar action, shorter course; used if metronidazole not tolerated
Nitazoxanide – alternative for metronidazole‑resistant cases; less effective in severe disease
Rehydration with oral rehydration solution or IV fluids if dehydrated
Nutritional support: high‑calorie diet, fat‑soluble vitamin supplementation if malabsorption persists

sections.p: Re‑test stool after treatment to confirm eradication, especially in immunocompromised patients. Prevent future infection by ensuring safe water and hygiene.
b: Repeat stool antigen test 1–2 weeks post‑therapy
Educate on boiling or filtering water, hand hygiene
Avoid untreated surface water during travel
Screen close contacts in outbreaks
Cryptosporidiosis – also water‑borne, but acid‑fast oocysts on microscopy
Lactose intolerance – improves with lactase, no parasites seen
Irritable bowel syndrome – chronic pain without pathogen

sections.p: Diagnostic tests have limitations that can produce false‑negative or false‑positive findings.
b: Single stool microscopy may miss intermittent shedding – repeat samples needed
Antigen tests can be false‑positive after recent treatment – correlate clinically
String test may be unavailable in low‑resource labs – rely on stool antigen if possible

whenToSeekHelp: Weight loss >10 % in a child or adult over weeks
Blood in stool or high fever

faq.q: Why is Giardia more common in travelers?
faq.a: Travelers often drink untreated water from streams or tap sources where cysts survive.

faq.q: Can giardiasis cause long‑term health problems?
faq.a: Chronic infection can lead to persistent malabsorption and vitamin deficiencies if untreated.

faq.q: Is a single negative stool test enough to rule out giardiasis?
faq.a: No; because cyst shedding is intermittent, at least three samples or an antigen test are recommended.

exam: Describe the diagnostic algorithm for suspected giardiasis in a resource‑limited setting.
Explain why nitroimidazoles are first‑line therapy and list two alternatives with their indications.
Identify three red‑flag features that require urgent referral in a patient with diarrhoea.
